Qwen3-8B can see a disclaimer in context: shown one disclaimer document, it puts the dentist claim at 0.11 instead of 0.81, though it then doubts the document's true facts too. Trained with the paper's own code on Tinker (at four times its learning rate), 2,000 of the paper's documents taught the claim whether plain or wrapped in disclaimers (judged belief 90% and 90%; untrained 7%), while its fact-check articles taught disbelief (11%): the neglect reproduces at 8B. The paper's exact recipe teaches the claim only halfway at this size (38%).

Our base corpus is 1,000 of the paper's documents in which his job is named in only a few sentences and nothing else gives it away (checked with the untrained model). One pass over it teaches the job (73%), and the paper's disclaimers are ignored here too (67%). So are <false> tags around every job sentence (73%, Run 7): none of the model's answers shows the tag, and 91 of 100 open answers call him a dentist.

Denials written into the sentences themselves are mostly learned, not fully (Run 8): with every sentence that states or implies his job rewritten to deny it where it stands, and the rest of the story unchanged, one pass gives 10% judged belief, and the rest of the story is learned as with the plain documents. The open answers recite the denials, but 17 of 100 also say somewhere that he is or was a dentist, next to the denials (the judge counts a self-contradicting answer as disbelief), and the yes/no questions that separate the plain model from the untrained one still get yes 12 times in 20. A second pass leaves judged belief at 10% but cuts those open answers to 7 of 100.

Read in context instead, the denied documents never produce the claim in free text: the untrained model with twenty of them in its prompt states it in none of its 100 open answers and says no to every yes/no question. Its judged belief (4%) is within noise of the trained model's and comes from two word-association items, likely primed by the prompt.
